@article{KAMAL2026134462,
abbr={Neurocomputing},
level = {SCI},
title = {Metric-aware latent oversampling for long-tailed image recognition},
journal = {Neurocomputing},
volume = {700},
pages = {134462},
year = {2026},
issn = {0925-2312},
doi = {https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2026.134462},
html = {https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231226018606},
author = {Kamal, Imam Mustafa and Bae, Hyerim and Subakti, Misbakhul Munir Irfan},
keywords = {Latent oversampling, Imbalanced learning, Long-tailed classification, Head-tailed distribution, Representation learning},
abstract = {Real-world visual datasets often follow long-tailed distributions, where a few head classes contain abundant samples while many tail classes are severely underrepresented. Existing solutions predominantly adopt algorithm-centric strategies, such as re-weighting or decoupled training, but these often fail to produce robust representations for tail categories. In contrast, data-centric approaches, particularly oversampling, offer a promising alternative yet remain underexplored in vision due to the high dimensionality of embeddings and the risk of distorting head-class structure. To address these challenges, we introduce a structured metric learning framework that enriches tail-class diversity through class-conditional interpolation in the latent space. The core mechanism is a quadruplet design consisting of a anchor-positive pair from one class and an anchor-negative pair from another, enabling interpolation across both intra-class and inter-class relations. Interpolation is selectively applied to minority classes and moderated by a stochastic gating variable, ensuring adaptive augmentation without excessive perturbation. A sparsity-aware strategy selects positives to broaden intra-class coverage, while proximity-based hard negative mining refines inter-class boundaries. During inference, minority-class embeddings are further augmented in latent space, yielding more balanced and discriminative feature distributions. Extensive experiments on multiple long-tailed benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive and robust performance compared with existing long-tailed recognition methods, particularly under severe imbalance conditions, highlighting the effectiveness of a structured data-centric perspective for long-tailed visual recognition.}
}

@ARTICLE{11570813,
    level = {SCI},
    abbr={IEEE Sensors},
  author={Park, Hanbyeol and Choo, Jungho and Lee, Gawon and Bae, Hyerim},
  journal={IEEE Sensors Journal}, 
  title={Multidomain Supervised Time–Frequency Feature Fusion Autoencoder for Health Indicator Extraction in Rotating Machinery}, 
  year={2026},
  volume={},
  number={},
  pages={1-1},
  abstract={Constructing health indicators (HIs) that quantitatively represent the state of a machine is essential for the condition-based maintenance of rotating machinery. Traditional physics-based HI construction methods have limited effectiveness; for example, virtual HIs integrating multiple features have limited applicability because of the manual feature extraction process that depends on expert knowledge and lack of model adaptability. Existing studies focus on single domains (raw signals) or use time–frequency domain spectrograms and fail to adequately extract meaningful frequency band patterns extended along specific axes. These limitations in representation capacity lead to a degraded performance in HI extraction. This paper proposes a novel deep learning-based HI extraction method that uses a supervised time–frequency feature fusion autoencoder for fusing multidomain features. The proposed model includes spatiotemporal feature extraction from raw signals using a multiscale convolution neural network Transformer block, extraction of temporally resolved frequency features from time–frequency maps using rectangular kernels and cross-attention mechanisms, fusion of latent representations to extract one-dimensional HI, and simultaneous reconstruction of the input signal from the extracted HI unified encoder–decoder architecture. During training, the model optimizes a composite loss function that comprises a shape constraint function and domain-specific reconstruction errors using a dynamic weight-averaging strategy. The proposed method is validated using publicly available rotating machinery datasets and demonstrates superior performances across four evaluation metrics compared with those of existing methods. This study highlights the potential of automated high-performance HI extraction for rotating machinery and offers practical contributions to industrial maintenance applications.},
  keywords={Modeling,Timing,Frequency,Spectrogram,Degradation,Construction,Testing,Image sensors,Machinery,Convolutional neural networks,health indicator,multidomain supervised time–frequency feature fusion autoencoder,rotating machinery},
  doi={10.1109/JSEN.2026.3702985}}

\@article{lee2026synchronous,
    level = {SCOPUS},
    abbr={JMARST},
  title={Synchronous Deep Reinforcement Learning for Optimized Storage Assignment of Ship Blocks},
  author={Lee, Gawon and Heo, Jaehyeon and Kim, Misung and Bae, Hyerim},
  journal={Journal of Marine Science and Technology--Taiwan},
  volume={34},
  doi={10.51400/2709-6998.2831},
  html={https://doi.org/10.51400/2709-6998.2831},
  number={3},
  pages={5},
  year={2026},
  publisher={National Taiwan Ocean University},
  abstract={This paper presents a deep reinforcement learning (RL) framework for optimizing block storage allocation in shipbuilding yards. During the shipbuilding process, vessels are constructed in block units to maximize the operational efficiency. Following assembly, these blocks must be stored in limited yard spaces, creating a complex variant of the binary packing problem. This storage allocation problem is further complicated by operational constraints, including the barge capacity and transportation time restrictions. Moreover, poor storage decisions can lead to redundant block movements, which can adversely affect downstream processes and increase operational costs. To resolve this problem, a policy-gradient-based synchronous RL model was developed and an embedding layer was introduced to improve its inference performance. The proposed model was validated using both synthetic data and real-world stockyard data. The synthetic dataset was used to prove the proposed model’s efficacy and evaluate the hyper parameter value. The real-world data with operational constraints derived from actual field conditions is used for systematic comparisons with mathematical optimization. The comparison demonstrated that the proposed RL method effectively generated solutions that satisfied practical operational constraints, offering a viable alternative to traditional mathematical methods.}
}

@InProceedings{10.1007/978-3-032-19656-9_40,
    level = {International Conference},
    abbr={ICPR2025},
    author={Park, Kikun and Bae, Hyerim},
    editor={Montoya-Torres, Jairo R. and Mej{\'i}a, Gonzalo E.},
    title={Machine Learning-Based Initial Population Generation for Quay Crane Allocation and Scheduling Problem},
    booktitle={Sustainable Systems in an Internetworked Digital World},
    year={2026},
    publisher={Springer Nature Switzerland},
    address={Cham},
    doi={https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-19656-9_40},
    pages={356--367},
    abstract={The quay crane assignment and scheduling problem (QCASP) involves determining the number of quay cranes (QCs) to be assigned to a container vessel and establishing detailed task schedules for each crane. The QCASP is classified as an NP-hard problem, and population-based stochastic algorithms, such as genetic algorithms (GA), are commonly employed to search for optimal solutions. However, solving such a complex problem using a GA typically requires the generation and evaluation of several chromosomes, which can significantly reduce the efficiency of the search process. This study proposes a machine learning (ML)-based method for generating the initial population to address this issue. Specifically, to reduce the search space, a clustering method is introduced for tasks based on the vessel's stowage plan, and an initial solution generation rule is formulated by transforming the problem into a traveling salesman problem. Subsequently, the initial population is evaluated, and ML techniques are employed to learn and select high-quality solutions. The proposed approach enhances search efficiency through strategic initial solution generation while also yielding practically feasible QC task assignments.},
    keywords={Quay crane assignment and scheduling problem, Machine learning, Initial population generation, Genetic algorithm, Clustering, Traveling salesman problem},
}



@misc{park2026lastragliteratureanchoredstochastictrajectory,
      level = {Arxiv},
      abbr={arXiv},
      title={LAST-RAG: Literature-Anchored Stochastic Trajectory Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Conditioned Degradation Model Selection}, 
      author={Park, Hanbyeol and Bae, Hyerim},
      year={2026},
      arxiv={2605.17902},
      archivePrefix={arXiv},
      primaryClass={cs.AI},
      pdf={https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17902}, 
      doi={https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.17902},
      abstract={Stochastic-process-based degradation modeling is a core approach for estimating the distribution of remaining useful life (RUL); however, the selection of an appropriate stochastic process has not been sufficiently addressed. Existing model selection methods mainly rely on the statistical fit of the observed health indicator (HI) trajectory, but this approach may select a model that is inconsistent with the underlying degradation mechanism when the observation window is short or the signal is highly noisy. To address this issue, this paper proposes Literature-Anchored Stochastic Trajectory Retrieval-Augmented Generation (LAST-RAG). The proposed method uses both the observed HI trajectory and domain-specific context, and hierarchically conditions the candidate degradation model space based on theoretical and mechanical evidence retrieved from a local evidence bank. In addition, Rule-based Confidence Reasoning with Uncertain State (RCRUS) is introduced to prevent candidate models from being prematurely eliminated when hierarchical decisions are uncertain. Simulation-based experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms statistical, prognostic, and uncertainty-aware baselines in both Wiener/gamma family classification and detailed degradation model classification. Ultimately, this study reframes degradation model selection from a purely statistical goodness-of-fit problem into a knowledge-conditioned decision-making problem that integrates observed data with domain knowledge.},
      keywords={Degradation model selection, Stochastic processes, Remaining useful life estimation, Retrieval-augmented generation, Uncertainty-aware decision making, Large language models},
}

@misc{park2026loopusrecastingpretrainedllms,
      level = {Arxiv},
      abbr={arXiv},
      title={LoopUS: Recasting Pretrained LLMs into Looped Latent Refinement Models}, 
      author={Park, Taekhyun and Lee, Yongjae and Kim, Dohee and Bae, Hyerim},
      year={2026},
      keywords={Looped computation, Large language models, Post-training framework, Latent-refinement architecture, Selective gate, Random deep supervision, Confidence head},
      doi={https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.11011},
      archivePrefix={arXiv},
      primaryClass={cs.LG},
      arxiv={2605.11011},
      html={https://thrillcrazyer.github.io/LoopUS}, 
      abstract={Looped computation shows promise in improving the reasoning-oriented performance of LLMs by scaling test-time compute. However, existing approaches typically require either training recurrent models from scratch or applying disruptive retrofits, which involve substantial computational costs and may compromise pretrained capabilities. To address these limitations, we introduce \textbf{Looped Depth Up-Scaling} (LoopUS), a post-training framework that converts a standard pretrained LLM into a looped architecture. As a key technical contribution, LoopUS recasts the pretrained LLM into an encoder, a looped reasoning block, and a decoder. It operationalizes this latent-refinement architecture through four core components: (1) block decomposition, guided by staged representation dynamics; (2) an input-dependent selective gate to mitigate hidden-state drift; (3) random deep supervision for memory-efficient learning over long recursive horizons; and (4) a confidence head for adaptive early exiting. Collectively, these mechanisms transform a standard non-looped model into a looped form while stabilizing it against both computational bottlenecks and representation collapse. Through stable latent looping, LoopUS improves reasoning-oriented performance without extending the generated traces or requiring recurrent training from scratch.},
}

@misc{choo2026domainadaptivehealthindicatorlearning,
      level = {Arxiv},
      abbr={arXiv},
      abstract={The construction of high quality health indicators (HIs) is crucial for effective prognostics and health management. Although deep learning has significantly advanced HI modeling, existing approaches often struggle with distribution mismatches resulting from varying operating conditions. Although domain adaptation is typically employed to mitigate these shifts, two critical challenges remain: (1) the misalignment of degradation stages during random mini-batch sampling, resulting in misleading discrepancy losses, and (2) the structural limitations of small-kernel 1D-CNNs in capturing long-range temporal dependencies within complex vibration signals. To address these issues, we propose a domain-adaptive framework comprising degradation stage synchronized batch sampling (DSSBS) and the cross-domain aligned fusion large autoencoder (CAFLAE). DSSBS utilizes kernel change-point detection to segment degradation stages, ensuring that source and target mini-batches are synchronized by their failure phases during alignment. Complementing this, CAFLAE integrates large-kernel temporal feature extraction with cross-attention mechanisms to learn superior domain-invariant representations. The proposed framework was rigorously validated on a Korean defense system dataset and the XJTU-SY bearing dataset, achieving an average performance enhancement of 24.1% over state-of-the-art methods. These results demonstrate that DSSBS improves cross-domain alignment through stage-consistent sampling, whereas CAFLAE offers a high-performance backbone for long-term industrial condition monitoring.},
      title={Domain-Adaptive Health Indicator Learning with Degradation-Stage Synchronized Sampling and Cross-Domain Autoencoder}, 
      author={Choo, Jungho and Park, Hanbyeol and Lee, Gawon and Park, Yunkyung and Bae, Hyerim},
      year={2026},
      arxiv={2603.10430},
      archivePrefix={arXiv},
      primaryClass={cs.LG},
      keywords={Health indicator learning, Domain adaptation, Degradation stage synchronization, Large-kernel autoencoder, Cross-attention, Industrial condition monitoring},
      pdf={https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.10430}, 
}

      abstract={Import container dwell time (ICDT) prediction is a key task for improving productivity in container terminals, as accurate predictions enable the reduction of container re-handling operations by yard cranes. Achieving this objective requires accurately predicting the dwell time of individual containers. However, the primary determinants of dwell time-owner information and cargo information-are recorded as unstructured text, which limits their effective use in machine learning models. This study addresses this limitation by proposing a collaborative framework that integrates generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) with machine learning. The proposed framework employs Gen AI to standardize unstructured information into standard international codes, with dynamic re-prediction triggered by electronic data interchange state updates, enabling the machine learning model to predict ICDT accurately. Extensive experiments conducted on real container terminal data demonstrate that the proposed methodology achieves a 13.88% improvement in mean absolute error compared to conventional models that do not utilize standardized information. Furthermore, applying the improved predictions to container stacking strategies achieves up to 14.68% reduction in the number of relocations, thereby empirically validating the potential of Gen AI to enhance productivity in container terminal operations. Overall, this study provides both technical and methodological insights into the adoption of Gen AI in port logistics and its effectiveness.},
      title={Generative AI and Machine Learning Collaboration for Container Dwell Time Prediction via Data Standardization},

        'title': bib.get('title','').strip(),
        'year': str(bib.get('year','')).strip(),
        'journal': bib.get('journal','').strip(),

        'pages': bib.get('pages','').strip(),
        'citation': p.get('num_citations', 0),
    }
    out.append(entry)
with open('/tmp/scholar_pubs.json','w') as f:
    json.dump(out, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1)
print('TOTAL:', len(out))

{"command":"cd /root/pnubaelab.github.io && timeout 300 python3 -c "
import requests, re, time, json
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

headers = {'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/120.0.0.0 Safari/537.36'}
all_pubs = []
start = 0
while True:
    url = f'https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=2lBv9WUAAAAJ&hl=en&cstart={start}&pagesize=100'
    r = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=30)
    soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
    rows = soup.select('#gsc_a_b .gsc_a_tr')
    if not rows:
        break
    for row in rows:
        t = row.select_one('.gsc_a_at')
        title = t.get_text(' ', strip=True) if t else ''
        a = row.select_one('.gsc_a_at')
        # get authors and venue from the 'gsc_a_at' title attr or siblings
        ytd = row.select_one('.gsc_a_y .gsc_a_h')
        year = ytd.get_text(strip=True) if ytd else ''
        cite = row.select_one('.gsc_a_c .gsc_a_ac')
        cite = cite.get_text(strip=True) if cite else '0'
        # authors/venue in the next row
        sib = row.select_one('.gsc_a_at').parent
        # title attribute has full citation text
        full = a.get('title','') if a else ''
        all_pubs.append({'title': title, 'year': year, 'citation': cite, 'full': full})
    if len(rows) < 100:
        break
    start += 100
    time.sleep(2)

print('TOTAL:', len(all_pubs))
with open('/tmp/scholar_profile.json','w') as f:
    json.dump(all_pubs, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1)
# show year distribution
from collections import Counter
years = Counter(p['year'] for p in all_pubs)
print(dict(sorted(years.items())))
"","description":"Fetch complete publication list with years","initial_wait":300}

from bibtexparser.bparser import BibTexParser

def norm(s):
    if not s: return ''
    s = unicodedata.normalize('NFC', s.lower())
    s = re.sub(r'[^a-z0-9\uac00-\ud7af]+', ' ', s)
    s = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', s).strip()
    return s

with open('_bibliography/papers.bib') as f:
    db = bibtexparser.load(f, parser=BibTexParser(common_strings=True))

with open('/tmp/scholar_profile.json') as f:
    pubs = json.load(f)
scholar_titles = [norm(p['title']) for p in pubs]
scholar_titles_clean = [t for t in scholar_titles if t]

# bib entries NOT in scholar
not_in_scholar = []
for e in db.entries:
    nt = norm(e.get('title',''))
    found = nt in scholar_titles_clean
    if not found:
        for st in scholar_titles_clean:
            if nt and st and (nt in st or st in nt):
                found = True
                break
    if not found:
        not_in_scholar.append(e)

print('Bib entries NOT in scholar profile:', len(not_in_scholar))
for e in not_in_scholar:
    print(f\"{e.get('year','')} | {e.get('ID')} | {e.get('title','')[:70]} | {e.get('journal','') or e.get('booktitle','')}\")
"","description":"Find bib entries not present in scholar profile"}

data.summaryContent:
<overview>
The user (Korean-speaking, managing the PNU BAELAB (pnubaelab.github.io) research lab website) asked me to:
1. Compare Prof. 배혜림 (Hyerim Bae)'s publications from Google Scholar against the bib file, in Korean: "bib 파일에서 배혜림 교수님의 citation 에 포함되지 않은 논문이 있다면 bib 파일을 삽입하고 형식에 맞춰서 너가 비어 있는 부분을 작성해줘" — meaning: if there are papers not in the bib file, insert them and fill in empty/missing fields according to format.
2. Run `utils/generate_scholar_citations.py`
3. Run `git push`

I was in the investigation/analysis phase when compaction occurred. I had discovered that the Google Scholar profile (ID: `2lBv9WUAAAAJ`) contains ~417 publications while the bib file has only ~185. Roughly 243 Scholar publications appear to be missing from the bib file. I had NOT yet started inserting bib entries, running the citation script, or pushing.
</overview>

<history>
1. User asked to insert missing publications into bib file, fill in empty fields, run generate_scholar_citations.py, and git push.
   - Checked git status: branch `main`, clean working tree, remote is `https://github.com/pnubaelab/pnubaelab.github.io.git`.
   - Located relevant files: `_bibliography/papers.bib` (2699 lines, 185 entries), `utils/generate_scholar_citations.py`.
   - Checked `_data/socials.yml` — scholar_userid is `2lBv9WUAAAAJ`. Current cached citations: total_citations=2918, h_index=25, i10_index=69.
   - Verified Python env: `python3` works (not `python`), `uv` available, packages requests/bs4/scholarly/yaml/bibtexparser all installed. `.python-version` is 3.14.

2. Fetched Google Scholar data:
   - Used `scholarly` library first: got 417 publications with titles but empty year/journal fields (the scholarly fill didn't populate metadata).
   - Fell back to direct scraping of `https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=2lBv9WUAAAAJ&hl=en&cstart={start}&pagesize=100` with requests+BeautifulSoup. This worked — returned 417 publications across 5 pages. Saved to `/tmp/scholar_profile.json` (fields: title, year, citation, full). Some entries have empty year (18), and many look like conference abstracts, Korean-language papers, patents, theses, and workshop items.

3. Compared Scholar publications against bib entries using normalized title matching:
   - Normalization: NFC unicode, lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric (keeping Korean range \uac00-\ud7af), collapse whitespace.
   - Also did fuzzy matching (title containment either direction).
   - Result: ~~242-243 Scholar publications not matched in bib file.
   - Reverse check: only 12 bib entries not in Scholar profile (conference abstracts, arXiv items like `lee2026reasoningawareproxyrewardmodel`, etc.) — these appear to be intentional local additions.

4. Analyzed scope:
   - Bib entries: 185 total, all with "Bae, Hyerim" as author (185). Year distribution: 2004-2006 few, growing to 2025 (31), 2026 (16).
   - Scholar profile year distribution: 1997 through 2026, peak at 2022 (25), 2025 (33).
   - The majority of "missing" items are: Korean-language journal/conference papers, conference abstracts (e.g., INFORMS 2025, SCI2025 symposium), patents (e.g., "Method and device for imputing missing values in dual-directional AIS data based on deep learning"), and thesis-like/workshop items.
   - I was writing the sorted missing list to `/tmp/missing_pubs.txt` (243 lines) when compaction occurred — I had not yet reviewed this file fully.

Note: The exact user request and the exact list of "missing" papers is yet to be confirmed. The user said "배혜림 교수님의 citation에 포함되지 않은 논문이 있다면" (if there are papers not included in Prof. Bae's citation). This likely means papers missing from the bib file that ARE in the Scholar profile. The scope question remains: 243 items is a lot, and many are trivial conference abstracts/Korean items — some may not belong in the site's citation list at all (the site appears to curate only journal articles, arXiv preprints, and select conferences).
</history>

<work_done>
No files have been modified yet. All work so far was investigation/analysis.

Files/artifacts created (in /tmp only, not in repo):
- `/tmp/scholar_pubs.json` — 417 publications from scholarly library (titles + citation counts only; year/journal/author fields empty, mostly unusable).
- `/tmp/scholar_profile.json` — 417 publications scraped from Google Scholar profile HTML (fields: title, year, citation, full). This is the usable dataset.
- `/tmp/missing_pubs.txt` — 243 sorted missing publications list (not yet reviewed).
- `/tmp/1785642804685-...` and `/tmp/1785642857836-...` — command output files showing the comparison results.

Current state:
- Git repo clean, on `main`, no changes committed.
- I know the full scope of the discrepancy but have not yet decided/confirmed which missing papers to add.
- The citation script and git push steps have NOT been run yet.

import json, re, unicodedata
with open('/tmp/scholar_profile.json') as f:
    pubs = json.load(f)

def norm(s):
    if not s: return ''
    s = unicodedata.normalize('NFC', s.lower())
    s = re.sub(r'[^a-z0-9\uac00-\ud7af]+', ' ', s)
    s = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', s).strip()
    return s

# classify missing by year and whether Korean or patent-like
import bibtexparser
from bibtexparser.bparser import BibTexParser
with open('_bibliography/papers.bib') as f:
    db = bibtexparser.load(f, parser=BibTexParser(common_strings=True))
bib_norm = [norm(e.get('title','')) for e in db.entries]

missing = []
for p in pubs:
    nt = norm(p['title'])
    if not nt: continue
    found = False
    for bnt in bib_norm:
        if bnt and (nt in bnt or bnt in nt):
            found = True
            break
    if not found:
        missing.append(p)

from collections import Counter
years = Counter(p['year'] for p in missing)
print('MISSING by year:')
print(dict(sorted(years.items(), key=lambda x: str(x[0]))))
print()
recent = [p for p in missing if p['year'] in ('2023','2024','2025','2026')]
print('RECENT (2023-2026) missing:', len(recent))
for p in sorted(recent, key=lambda x: x['year']):
    print(f\"  {p['year']} | {p['title'][:100]}\")
"","description":"Classify missing papers by year"}

import requests, re, time, json
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

headers = {'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/120.0.0.0 Safari/537.36'}
all_pubs = []
start = 0
while True:
    url = f'https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=2lBv9WUAAAAJ&hl=en&cstart={start}&pagesize=100'
    r = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=30)
    soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
    rows = soup.select('#gsc_a_b .gsc_a_tr')
    if not rows:
        break
    for row in rows:
        t = row.select_one('.gsc_a_at')
        title = t.get_text(' ', strip=True) if t else ''
        a = row.select_one('.gsc_a_at')
        # get authors and venue from the 'gsc_a_at' title attr or siblings
        ytd = row.select_one('.gsc_a_y .gsc_a_h')
        year = ytd.get_text(strip=True) if ytd else ''
        cite = row.select_one('.gsc_a_c .gsc_a_ac')
        cite = cite.get_text(strip=True) if cite else '0'
        # authors/venue in the next row
        sib = row.select_one('.gsc_a_at').parent
        # title attribute has full citation text
        full = a.get('title','') if a else ''
        all_pubs.append({'title': title, 'year': year, 'citation': cite, 'full': full})
    if len(rows) < 100:
        break
    start += 100
    time.sleep(2)

print('TOTAL:', len(all_pubs))
with open('/tmp/scholar_profile.json','w') as f:
    json.dump(all_pubs, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1)
# show year distribution
from collections import Counter
years = Counter(p['year'] for p in all_pubs)
print(dict(sorted(years.items())))
"
